entries.title: DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate
entries.summary: The DOJ also filed an emergency request in federal court to stop California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls the federal government says are "likely noncitizens."
entries.content:
DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate

The Justice Department announced on Monday it was charging 28 noncitizens with election crimes in California, signaling a further escalation over the state's voting system that looks like it will continue through Election Day and beyond.

The DOJ also filed an emergency request in federal court to stop California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls whom the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." The state has asked for specific information on how the federal government came to its conclusions, but has not received it.

"This Department of Justice will not look the other way while noncitizens vote in federal elections," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said at a press conference on Monday announcing the election crime charges. "Unfortunately the same can't be said for California and L.A. County."

Noncitizen voting has never been found to be a widespread problem in American elections, but the Trump administration is devoting significant resources to uncovering the ineligible voting that does occur. The DOJ has been announcing handfuls of new charges almost every day as early voting gets underway in many states.

The Justice Department's latest request in federal court is a continuation of a saga that began this summer with President Trump's primetime speech on election integrity. It took a major turn last week with the delivery of a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them. Local and state officials declined to do so, and the federal government sued.

McCotter escalated the dispute further on Friday by warning California officials in a letter that they could be criminally prosecuted for knowingly processing ballots "cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens." President Trump wrote on Truth Social that evening: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

Taken together, the threats have local officials and election experts worried that the adversarial posture of the Justice Department towards California portends more actions to come aimed at delegitimizing results in this fall's midterms.

"There's a few things to be worried about," said Rick Hasen, an election law expert who runs UCLA's Safeguarding Democracy Project. "One is the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters. The other is the risk that it further undermines voter confidence in the electoral process by making it seem like [noncitizen voting] is a major problem when it is not. And the third risk is that this is going to be used as some sort of pretext to try to seize ballots or interfere after the election is over."

Dana Lewis, the Republican county recorder for Pinal County, Ariz., said local officials nationwide are watching and communicating about what's happening in California, the same way they did when the FBI raided an elections office in Fulton County, Ga. in January.

If those officials are administering a race this fall that is close or contested, they feel they could be next, she said.

"When this impacts another jurisdiction, you automatically have to feel that," Lewis said. "If it's happening in Georgia, if it's happening in Colorado or California, we're all watching."

New criminal charges against noncitizens in California

All 28 people charged in California on Monday are green-card holders, and all appeared on the list of 20,000 names the DOJ gave California officials last week, according to DOJ officials.

A number of them do not appear to have actually voted, and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago. Many are accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications, which ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship.

Previous research has shown that when noncitizen voting and registration occurs, it is also often the result of bureaucratic error and not intentional fraud. New Jersey revealed this summer that a software glitch at the DMV registered more than 6,000 people to vote even though they had indicated they were noncitizens.

Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for California's Central District, downplayed that possibility on Monday, however.

"It's not something that just happens to you," Essayli said. "They either attested to it when they got a driver's license, or they went out of their way to file a voter registration form, and they swore under oath that they were a citizen."

In the past seven weeks, the Justice Department has charged 113 noncitizens across 20 states with voting and registration crimes, officials said at Monday's press conference.

UCLA's Hasen said the charges seem to be meant to make noncitizen voting "look like a bigger issue than it is."

"Given that there's over 20 million registered voters in California, this is quite a small number of allegations," Hasen said. "And we don't know how many of these allegations will even pan out. And so even if all of these were in fact people who were illegally voting, it's a drop in the bucket compared to the number of voters in California."

Recent polling suggests a sizable portion of the American public thinks immigration enforcement will be present at voting locations this fall, despite federal law banning armed federal agents from the polls. Non-white voters are more likely than white voters to say they fear voting could put them at risk of being questioned by immigration authorities despite being citizens.

In an interview earlier this fall with NPR, Los Angeles County's top voting official, Dean Logan, alluded to those worries.

"Given everything leading up to this election, what we're trying to remind voters is the best way to secure the election is through your participation," Logan told NPR. "Don't be distracted by the litigation. Don't be distracted by the mis- and disinformation. If you have questions, let us know, let us answer them. But don't let this keep you from voting," he said.

"Because if you're not voting, none of the rest matters, right?"

An unprecedented demand by DOJ

The Justice Department's request that a federal judge block California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots from the list of 20,000 "likely noncitizens" it gave state officials last week is unprecedented and an especially unusual request given that voting is already underway.

California officials have argued that complying with the Department's demand to set the ballots aside would be unlawful and noted the DOJ has not confirmed that the voters on the list are noncitizens.

"The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote to the DOJ's McCotter on Oct. 13.

"Withholding ballots from some duly registered voters and segregating and refusing to tabulate voted ballots submitted by others, is an unprecedented suspension — and even denial — of voting rights," she wrote.

Los Angeles County's assistant county counsel, Peter Bollinger, wrote to McCotter on Oct. 15: "we are not authorized to, or are prohibited from, taking the actions requested in your letter under both federal and state law. The actions described would disenfranchise those in question without due process." The same letter noted the list of names from the DOJ included voters from outside Los Angeles County, whom the office does not maintain any records on.

Both letters cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law that bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters from state voter rolls during the 90 days before an election. The law is supposed to prevent mistakes that could erroneously purge eligible voters right before an election without giving voters time to correct errors.

There are also questions about the methodology the Trump administration used to come up with its tally of 20,000 likely noncitizens and its accuracy. A July letter to California from the Department of Homeland Security alleged the state had a potential of 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls.

In Monday's press briefing, McCotter said the 20,000 figure represented the people the Justice Department had the most confidence were noncitizens after DHS cross-referenced various government databases and other records with identifying information.

McCotter and other DOJ officials blamed California for not handing over its entire voter roll — including partial Social Security Numbers and driver's license numbers — which they said could help shed more light on the citizenship status of these voters. So far 26 federal judges have dismissed DOJ demands for that data across the country.

In the Justice Department's Monday filing for a restraining order preventing California from counting ballots from the 20,000 individuals, the DOJ wrote: "Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm may be impossible to remedy. The urgency is heightened because of the fundamental right to vote and to have one's lawful vote counted without dilution."

A half dozen voting and civil rights organizations filed to intervene in the case last week to argue the DOJ's demands are unlawful.

Election experts have said the DOJ's lawsuit against California seems more about sending a political message or teeing up future challenges than winning this case in court, given that the constitution gives states the authority to administer elections.

"I expect this lawsuit to go nowhere," UCLA's Hasen wrote last week.

entries.title: Judge chastises Trump administration plan to push ahead overhaul of DC golf course
entries.summary: The Trump administration wants to turn a historic public golf course into championship links. Despite a judge's order, hundreds of trees were cut down to make way for the renovation.
entries.content:
Judge chastises Trump administration plan to push ahead overhaul of DC golf course

In a tense hearing on Monday, federal Judge Ana C. Reyes sharply rebuked administration lawyers over President Trump's apparent intent to defy the court and proceed with a major renovation of the historic East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C. Only days before, the judge had temporarily blocked the government from moving forward with the project.

During the hearing, which ended without a decision, Reyes chastised the government attorneys, who had previously told the court that renovating the links was still in its conceptual stage. So when Trump posted his detailed plans for a new golf course on Sunday, Reyes wanted to know who was responsible for misleading the court.

"Do I believe the president of the United States or do I believe you?" she asked.

During the hearing, Reyes frequently exhibited frustration and annoyance. "I have, on the one hand, the president of the United States saying to the American public three times now, I think, in the last two days, there is a final plan to redesign the golf course," she said. "Then I have you all telling me and, you know, witnesses saying what they're saying, that there's no final plan. Which is it?"

Trump has said that he wants to turn the three existing courses at the East Potomac Golf Links into a single, "championship-style golf course." But in February, a D.C. preservation group and two individuals challenged the U.S. Department of Interior and the National Park Service over the planned renovations, arguing that the renovated course would inflate tee-time costs for a facility that was originally intended to be "open to all people."

In May, the judge ordered the administration to give notice of any substantial construction work on the course, including the removal of more than 10 trees. Despite the order, late on Friday, Oct. 9 — just before a holiday weekend — government officials notified the court that it planned to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases.

Bulldozers began taking down hundreds of trees the next day. During a three-hour emergency hearing last week, Reyes called the government lawyers out for not giving enough prior notice for the tree removal. She did not believe the argument that the tree felling was part of routine maintenance, saying she was "beyond disappointed" by the action and ordered a 24-hour halt.

Judge: "Every single benefit of the doubt"

"I do not know how I could have made it any plainer that I did not want what was to happen, to happen," she said, adding: "I have given the government every single benefit of the doubt that it would not do precisely what it has done."

On Friday, the White House filed a motion requesting that Reyes remove herself from the case, accusing her of bias. The judge declined to step aside.

Ahead of the hearing on Monday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Reyes was a "crazed lunatic" and said that renovation work did not need court approval. "Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY!" he said. The president's post appears to contradict a response filed by Department of Justice lawyers the previous day indicating that "the plan is not final because the Park Service has not completed its review."

Trump has described the golf course as "old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect." The prospect of a complete renovation has alarmed residents who are concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.

A protected landmark

The century-old golf links were also one of the first public courses to be desegregated. "This is not just some putt-putt course," Reyes told the attorneys, who appeared in court on Monday. The park holds "a deep amount of meaning for the people of the district, and is protected as a historic landmark."

The White House has said that it is simply carrying out a 2019 preservation plan, but plaintiffs seeking to block the changes have said that Trump's stated desire to redevelop the course goes well beyond that. Among other things, the 2019 plan recommends removing invasive vegetation that doesn't contribute to the historic landscape, but not healthy, native species.

The golf course is one of several instances in which the president has sought to circumvent the courts in order to exert his power and to place his own stamp on Washington, D.C. He has also threatened to tear down the Kennedy Center and is seeking to build a 250-foot arch near the National Mall.

entries.title: Schools struggle to measure how much AI experiments are helping
entries.summary: Schools are experimenting with AI, and a lot of them are encountering the same problem: It's hard to measure whether the technology is good or bad for students.
entries.content:
Schools are experimenting with AI, and a lot of them are encountering the same problem: It's hard to measure whether the technology is good or bad for students.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

Schools across the country are experimenting with AI in classrooms. In some districts, AI chatbots give students feedback on their work. But how should schools measure whether these experiments are helping students or harming them? Lee Gaines reports from one school in Dayton, Ohio.

LEE GAINES, BYLINE: A high school senior is giving an angsty AI chatbot advice.

N: I feel like a therapist, like I'm actually helping him.

GAINES: The student, N, was part of an experiment last school year at the Alternative School at Jackson Center in Dayton. NPR is only using N's first initial because of the stigma associated with attending a school that serves students with behavioral challenges.

N: I kind of built this connection with him trying to get to the point of his issue and why he's, like, feeling this way.

GAINES: The him he's referring to is an AI chatbot named Jordan. Jordan asks students for advice, like what to do when you feel you can't meet adults' expectations. The idea is to get students to open up about their feelings.

N: I've been through similar things like Jordan, so it's - like, it's easier for me to try to help him get through it.

GAINES: The chatbot grades students' responses, and N gets high marks. There's just one problem - there's no way to quantify how much the chatbot is helping students. The best the district can do is ask students and staff.

MIKE KENTZ: Every test, every experiment that I try to measure in some sort of concrete way, I can only get as far as perception.

GAINES: Mike Kentz is a consultant who helped Dayton administrators design and evaluate the chatbot. He's been running into the same problem a lot of school AI experiments have encountered - it's hard to measure whether the technology is good or bad for students. Robin Lake leads the Center on Reinventing Public Education.

ROBIN LAKE: It's been frustrating to see that innovation is tackled without a lot of attention to evidence building.

GAINES: Lake's organization has been tracking AI adoption in schools. She says educators often struggle to measure the value of technology in classrooms, including when it comes to AI.

LAKE: The technology is moving so quickly. Tools are being produced at such a rapid pace. And everybody is feeling overwhelmed in schools and saying, you know, I don't know what works.

GAINES: That's one reason Mike Kentz is cautious about scaling up the Jordan chatbot in Dayton.

KENTZ: I don't think it should be immediately input into their district or any others as some sort of, you know, full-scale solution.

KATELYN SCHOENHOFER: We wrestle with what does success really mean when it comes to AI use.

GAINES: Katelyn Schoenhofer is the AI specialist for Wichita Public Schools in Kansas. The school system is slowly introducing students to a range of AI tools from a few different companies. Last year, the district hosted an AI exploration day for middle schoolers.

SCHOENHOFER: They got to make educational games and code those games and share them with their friends.

GAINES: And some high school students are using an AI math tutor. Until educators figure out how to measure the value of these AI initiatives, Schoenhofer says these experiments will remain small in scale, but they will continue.

SCHOENHOFER: We are still going ahead with caution but with optimism with our students because it is something that is going to impact their lives. It is something they need to be educated about.

GAINES: Robin Lake with the Center on Reinventing Public Education agrees that the answer isn't to stop experimenting because if that happens...

LAKE: We will set our kids back from being able to navigate a world that is changing outside of schools faster than we can possibly imagine.

GAINES: Lake says states and the federal government need to establish guardrails around these experiments so schools can try to prepare students for what's to come. For NPR News, I'm Lee Gaines.

(SOUNDBITE OF TYLER, THE CREATOR SONG, "ANSWER")

entries.title: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
entries.summary: A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.
entries.content:
Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'

MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.

Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.

Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.

The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.

"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.

"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.

Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.

Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.

In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.

entries.title: 2026 midterms could be the most expensive on record. And, Macron condemns protests
entries.summary: More than $15 billion has been raised in this year's midterm elections. And, France's president is condemning the violent protests erupting across the country.
entries.content:
Trump Eases Russia Sanctions, Midterm Campaign Money, Violent Protests In France

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The 2026 midterm elections are set to become the most expensive on record. More than $15 billion has been raised to influence the outcome and control of Congress.

  • 🎧 Democratic nominees in House and Senate races are raking in incredible amounts of donations, even though the Democratic Party remains unpopular, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Republicans are also unpopular, largely due to issues like the war in Iran, gas prices and the economy. A few megadonors, such as Elon Musk, are donating money to super PACs to try to push voters to elect Republicans. In the 13 competitive races highlighted in the Cook Political Report, Republicans are being outraised by a 5-to-1 margin. Both parties are spending heavily, indicating that Democrats might have a chance to win in several locations. Currently, 75% of planned ad buys are in toss-up races or those leaning Republican.
  • ➡️ Some of the most competitive congressional races might not be called until days after Election Day. Here's why.
  • ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

At least one person died and more than a dozen were injured in a major Ukrainian drone strike yesterday on Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital. The attack targeted strategic sites, including a key port oil terminal. Over the weekend, Russian missile strikes in Ukraine killed at least 11 people. This conflict continues as President Trump says that relieving pressure on Russia is the best way to end the war.

  • 🎧 The recent attack on Saint Petersburg appears to mark the largest one on the city since Russia's 2022 invasion, NPR's Charles Maynes tells Up First. While it's unclear how many drones struck the city, Russia's Defense Ministry reported intercepting 1,000 drones across various regions that night. Trump seems to be working to protect Russian oil facilities after cutting a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel. The move was aimed at lowering gas prices for U.S. voters before the midterm elections. Trump has called previous Ukrainian strikes a "disgrace," even as Russia continues to strike Ukraine, Maynes says. He adds that the president blames President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacks that allegedly raise U.S. fuel prices, despite economists attributing the price increase mainly to Trump's war in Iran.

French President Emmanuel Macron denounced violence over the weekend that he says has overshadowed largely peaceful protests across the country. The unrest began as a student protest for better conditions and has expanded to include public-sector workers protesting high energy prices, the rising cost of living and social inequality. The Interior Ministry reported about 2,300 arrests and nearly 1,000 injured police officers.

  • 🎧 NPR's Eleanor Beardsley, who was in the streets of Paris yesterday, witnessed burned bikes, shattered glass and graffiti on looted stores saying things like "tax the rich." She spoke with 23-year-old Sarah Berlia, who says she believes these actions come from a frustrated generation facing dwindling rights and opportunities. Beardsley says the protest culture in France often attracts "troublemakers," but the scale of current events is massive. The protests have had political implications, as France is six months away from a presidential election. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has joined the protesters, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, has condemned the violence and the government.

Living better

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Saunas are gaining renewed attention in the wellness world for their potential to improve mental health. This trend reflects the growing interest in the broader wellness movement and social connection, especially post-pandemic. While scientists understand how saunas affect the cardiovascular system, they are just beginning to explore their impact on mental health. Here's what they know so far.

  • 🥵 When our skin detects heat, it sends signals to a primitive brain area that prompts our body to cool down. This pathway also influences mood and pleasure, which is associated with depression.
  • 🥵 Heat triggers an anti-inflammatory response similar to the effects of exercise, which is known to help with depression and other mental health issues.
  • 🥵 Heating people up can act like a "thermoregulatory workout," helping their bodies cool down more efficiently over time.

Picture show

Artist Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has captured her family's everyday life through her lens for eight years, revealing moments of love, care and sacrifice within their Chicago home. The personal project took root in 2018, sparked by her grandmother's hospitalization. It started as a way to better understand her grandmother's daily routines, and soon it blossomed into a heartfelt exploration of the immigrant experience. "I am interested in what happens when the camera enters a home where everyone already knows one another," Villanueva told NPR. "There is no distance between photographer and subject. I am photographing the people who raised me, and I am also photographing the home that raised me." See photos from the project and read more about Villanueva's work.

3 things to know before you go

  • Noah Adams, a writer and broadcaster who hosted All Things Considered for 18 years, has died. He was 84 years old.
  • Trump announced over the weekend that he plans to close and renovate the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C. The golf course is already at the center of a legal battle.
  • An Air Force service member died Saturday after a rappelling accident during a pregame ceremony at the Alamodome ahead of the University of Texas at San Antonio's football game against Navy. (via Texas Public Radio)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

entries.title: A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming
entries.summary: A large underwater wave moved up the West Coast, raising sea levels. Scientists say it's driven by El Niño and it's going to happen again.
entries.content:
A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming

One of the first major signs of this year's "Super El Niño" has reached the U.S. It's called a Kelvin wave – a deep ocean wave that's currently raising sea levels along the West Coast.

Scientists have long known about Kelvin waves, but this year, the phenomena grabbed the public's attention with video explanations receiving thousands of views across TikTok and X.

"It does surprise me – I mean, here it's been around all this time," says Mark Cane, who created one of the first models to forecast and predict El Niño. "I'm sure Lord Kelvin is happy in his grave."

(Lord Kelvin, the British physicist who also developed the Kelvin temperature scale, first described the wave back in the late 1800s.)

Kelvin waves can develop along the equator during El Niño years, when a vast region of water in the Pacific Ocean becomes much warmer than usual.

Some of this warm water, in the form of a Kelvin wave that stretches thousands of miles, moves slowly east beneath the ocean's surface until it reaches South America. Then it splits, traveling north along the West Coast and as far south as Chile.

"It's like an enormous bathtub sloshing around," Cane says, professor emeritus of earth and climate sciences at Columbia University. "But the slosh is very peculiar, because it only goes west to east along the equator in a Kelvin wave."

These are not the massive, highly visible waves that crash into shorelines during major storms and hurricanes.

"It's not a wall of water, it's not a tsunami, it's not a wave you can surf," says Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor of atmospheric sciences at North Carolina State University. "It's a planetary-scale wave."

A Kelvin wave's impact is gradual, raising sea levels as it moves up the coast, and bringing with it an elevated risk of floods and warmer water temperatures.

What's the impact?

Kelvin waves can increase the risk of flooding and coastal erosion.

By themselves, Kelvin waves don't cause flooding, Amaya says. Instead, they load the dice, making flooding more likely by raising sea levels.

"It makes the background conditions more favorable towards coastal flooding, but what you need are triggering factors," Amaya said, such as a major storm or very high tides.

Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says Kelvin waves raise the chances of a "triple whammy" along the California coast: "El Nino, the high tide and the storm surge all coming at once."

That's exactly what some Southern California communities experienced in early October. Sea levels were already higher than normal because of the Kelvin wave – about six to eight inches, Amaya says. Then, when Tropical Storm Rachel hit, a storm surge flooded neighborhoods and left oceanfront homes partially submerged.

"That storm surge was almost certainly made more devastating because of the Kelvin wave," Amaya says.

Warmer water temperatures

Kelvin waves also bring warmer water up the coast, which can be disruptive and put stress on marine life.

"We've seen tropical fishes in places that we don't normally see them," Amaya says. "Like a whale shark was spotted off the coast of San Diego."

The Kelvin wave can push down nutrient-dense cold waters that support productive marine ecosystems. Amaya says researchers have already seen evidence of sea birds dying in response to warmer water temperatures along the coast.

When is the next Kelvin wave?

There are usually five to six Kelvin waves during a strong El Niño year, Amaya says.

Amaya predicts the next Kelvin wave will reach San Diego in late October or early November. Several more waves are expected through the fall and early winter, he says. Kelvin waves usually subside before the peak of El Niño.

The El Niño pattern typically peaks late in the year or early January. This year, NOAA researchers predict the El Niño will remain strong through early 2027.

entries.title: The real reason it's going to take a while to know who won in some midterm races
entries.summary: Hint: It's not only because California counts slowly.
entries.content:
Stephen Richer no longer runs elections in the fourth-largest county in the country.

But for the rest of his life, he'll remember the feeling when polls closed on an election night.

More than a million ballots staring at him and his staff. Every moment that passes without them fully counted means another conspiracy theory sprouting online.

"Those days, those were hell for me," said Richer, a Republican who served as the clerk and recorder for Arizona's Maricopa County. "You'd have a limited number of workers, and you'd have a limited amount of space, and you'd be doing everything that you possibly could. … And yet you have everyone blowing up your phone, everyone saying that you're incompetent or corrupt or worse."

This midterm year, election officials in competitive congressional districts will face that same pressure.

But they will also face a hard reality: that those races might not be called until days after Election Day.

Here's an FAQ on why that is, and what it could mean this year.

Why do we know the results immediately in some places, and in others it takes days or weeks?

It comes down to the margin of victory.

Which sounds strange, since who wins an election and by how much shouldn't impact how long it takes election officials to count ballots.

But the reality is what most Americans think of as "election results" — the winners announced on election nights across TV networks and social media — are not the result of all ballots being counted, but rather, races being called by news organizations that determine the winners based on a state or district's demographics and initial returns. (NPR relies on The Associated Press for its race calls.)

Those determinations come a lot faster when races aren't close.

"Margins matter," said Richer, who noted that in recent elections, there has been a lot less scrutiny on Utah than there has been on his home state of Arizona, or certain contests in California, despite the states counting votes at similar speeds.

"In Utah you can call all the races very quickly because the Republicans there have high margins," Richer said.

That gives the illusion of elections there being complete, but no state is done counting ballots on election night, even if it seems that way because notable races are called early.

Loading...

So you're saying the timing of results isn't at all tied to vote-counting speed?

Not exactly.

The closer the race, the more election analysts need to see before they can make a call. So the faster states count ballots, the faster those determinations can be made.

This is why the longest wait times every election usually come from places that have competitive races and which also count slowly.

Like, California?

Exactly. California has become the poster child for long results times because of both those factors: a bevy of competitive congressional districts, which help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House, and a vote count that's been among the slowest in the nation.

Add in that President Trump, the most prominent purveyor of election misinformation in the country, has long targeted the liberal California, and experts see a perfect storm for false voting narratives.

"It's progressive, it likes mail ballots, it gets [postmarked] mail ballots after Election Day," Richer said. "It just all adds up to a fairly incendiary situation."

Charles Stewart, an elections expert at MIT, put it more simply.

"California just has a big target on its back," said Stewart.

California's slow vote counting caused a lot of conspiracy theorizing during the state's June primary. Is this fall going to be a rerun?

Kim Alexander is cautiously optimistic that won't be the case.

She runs the California Voter Foundation, which has been advocating for ways to speed up California's vote tally without giving up the state's generous voting access policies, like mailing every active registered voter a ballot.

"We have all these amazing rights and opportunities that we give to our voters, and the price we're paying is a longer vote count," Alexander told NPR. "But that doesn't mean that it has to be this long."

The single biggest cause for California's slow count comes from a phenomenon Alexander calls "the pig in the python" problem: a logjam of millions of vote-by-mail ballots getting returned on Election Day that need to be processed.

Those ballots take longer to count than in-person votes, as officials need to deal with envelopes and verify signatures to make sure mail ballots are cast by the people they're supposed to be cast by.

Some counties see up to 50% of their vote-by-mail ballots turned in on Election Day, Alexander said, which means processing work doesn't even begin until later in the week.

"I can't tell you how many people who are informed and engaged and … when I tell them that the cause for the long vote count is voters holding on to their ballots to Election Day and turning them in, they look at me and they're like, 'That's what I do,'" Alexander said. "And I'm like, 'I know! You're part of the problem!'"

The state allocated $40 million to speeding up its counting this year, and part of that money is going to voter education.

Alexander is optimistic that once voters learn they can play a role in speeding up the process by voting earlier, or by utilizing other voting methods that allow for quicker counting, they will respond.

"California has been beaten up by this president for over a decade over our election process, and it's gotten pretty worrisome," Alexander said. "I think that California voters, if they feel they can do something to respond to that, many will take action."

To that point, research conducted earlier this year found that when voters in California's San Joaquin County received postcards urging them to vote earlier, they were more likely to meet the recommended deadline that allowed for election-night counting.

Alexander noted one more change that could mean less spotlight on California this year: fewer competitive House districts.

Ahead of the 2022 elections, the state had nine districts that the Cook Political Report considered competitive. But this year, in part because voters approved a mid-cycle gerrymander to respond to gerrymanders in Republican-controlled states, the state has just three.

That makes it less likely the entire country will be waiting on California to know who controls the House.

OK, anywhere else we should be watching when it comes to results speed?

Using the formula discussed earlier (competitive races + slow vote counting), it's impossible not to look at Alaska.

According to data from the MIT Election Lab, Alaska was the last state in 2024 to reach 95% of its ballots counted.

Election Day was Nov. 5 that year, but the state's lone House race — which Republican Nicholas Begich won by fewer than 10,000 votes — wasn't called by the AP until Nov. 20.

This year, polling shows a tight Alaska Senate race. That means, if results fall a certain way in other states, the entire country could be waiting weeks to know which party will control the U.S. Senate next year.

entries.title: Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigns in GOP stronghold
entries.summary: Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is campaigning in the GOP stronghold of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, an area that hasn't voted for a Democrat in Congress in over a decade.
entries.content:
Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed campaigns in GOP stronghold

Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El Sayed campaigns in GOP stronghold

Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is campaigning in the GOP stronghold of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, an area that hasn't voted for a Democrat in Congress in over a decade.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Back in the U.S., let's go to Michigan, where both of the Senate candidates have been focusing on urban areas with lots of voters, like Detroit and its suburbs. With about two weeks to go until Election Day, the Democrat in the race is also carrying his message into a Republican stronghold. Michigan Public Radio's Russ McNamara reports.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ABDUL EL-SAYED: How are we doing, Marquette?

RUSS MCNAMARA, BYLINE: Hundreds packed a rally on the campus of Northern Michigan University to hear Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's stump speech last week. It capped a whirlwind three-stop tour, covering a couple hundred miles across the state's rural and rugged Upper Peninsula. The goal for El-Sayed is to reach out to Yoopers, a nickname for people who live in the Upper Peninsula, or UP, and draw in support from conservatives. It's a tall order. Approximately 60% of them voted for Donald Trump two years ago. El-Sayed told reporters that he learned a lot from this campaign trip to the UP and a prior one in June.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

EL-SAYED: Yoopers are commonsense, thoughtful people, and they don't like paying more in gas than they need to, don't like paying more in groceries. And they don't like being taken advantage of by a billionaire from New York.

MCNAMARA: Still, Yoopers have a healthy skepticism for outsiders, according to Republican state representative Karl Bohnak. He's well known here. Before entering politics, Karl Bohnak was a TV meteorologist for about 30 years. He's backing the Republican candidate in this toss-up race, former Congressman Mike Rogers.

KARL BOHNAK: To be honest with you, I don't pay much attention to Abdul. I don't even really know what his message is. I think he meant something like Medicare for All. But the only question I would have is, who's going to pay for that?

MCNAMARA: Healthcare is an issue in the Upper Peninsula, with many having to drive 100 miles or more to see a specialist. Data from Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services show that nearly 1 in 3 UP residents are enrolled in Medicare, with 7% without insurance altogether. Bart Stupak was the last Democrat to represent the UP in the U.S. House choosing not to run for reelection in 2010. He endorsed Representative Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary but believes El-Sayed's messaging can resonate with Yoopers.

BART STUPAK: Just showing up helps him tremendously to try to connect with not just Democrats, but all the voters, even those Republicans who are disenchanted with the party right now.

MCNAMARA: Trips across rural Michigan are one part of a broader strategy to reach Republicans for El-Sayed.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

EL-SAYED: We got to be willing to invite them to a decision they have yet to make.

MCNAMARA: Speaking to a crowd in Escanaba, El-Sayed called on his supporters to connect with conservative family and friends to explain his key messages of Medicare for All and getting money out of politics.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

EL-SAYED: Reach out to them, OK? We have an opportunity to build our country, not just watch it get torn down.

MCNAMARA: While El-Sayed attempts to bridge a partisan gap, there is some hesitancy among moderates within his own party. In an interview late last week with Michigan Public Radio, former Congressman Stupak says some of El-Sayed's positions give him pause.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

STUPAK: I would have voted by now, but I just want to see how this plays out a little bit more. Yeah, I'm a Democrat, but that doesn't mean I vote for every Democrat that shows up on a ticket.

MCNAMARA: With razor-thin margins in this U.S. Senate race, rural conservatives would be a nice get for El-Sayed but mean little if he can't shore up his own base.

For NPR News, I'm Russ McNamara in Marquette, Michigan.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

entries.title: Solar power is changing agriculture in Pakistan, but some fear it could cause issues
entries.summary: Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear their widespread use could cause problems.
entries.content:
Solar power is changing agriculture in Pakistan, but some fear it could cause issues

Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear their widespread use could cause problems.

MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:

Solar power is transforming agriculture in Pakistan. Farmers are using it to run water pumps that lower their electricity costs and boost production. But in a country already facing water scarcity and extreme weather, some fear this will create new problems. Betsy Joles has more.

BETSY JOLES, BYLINE: Muhammad Abdullah (ph) stands alongside a tub full of minnows. It's part of the fish farm he helps run in Sallhoke Chatha, in Pakistan's Punjab province.

MUHAMMAD ABDULLAH: Maripa (ph) silver, bighead grass.

JOLES: He lists off some of the species wriggling in the water below. Once these fish are mature enough, they'll be moved to man-made ponds outside. The water in them needs to be changed frequently. Otherwise, the fish will die. For that, Abdullah uses well water pumped from the ground by a solar-powered motor. The pumps run for around 11 hours a day in the summer, cutting the farm's energy bill by about half.

ABDULLAH: (Non-English language spoken).

JOLES: Only those who have a lot of money can work without solar, Abdullah says. Many in this area got into fish farming because staple crops like wheat and corn didn't grow well there. Thanks to solar, access to groundwater has become much cheaper. But Mudassar Kharal, another fish farmer from the area, says no one is really keeping an eye on how much of it is being used.

MUDASSAR KHARAL: There is no check and balance.

JOLES: Some Pakistani water experts warned that solar-powered pumps could worsen the country's over-extraction of groundwater. Bashir Ahmad, director of the Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, says their use is particularly concerning in areas that are otherwise unfit for farming.

BASHIR AHMAD: Adoption of this saltwater pumping in those areas is really scary.

JOLES: Since 2023, there's been a push to cultivate some unproductive lands under the army-backed Green Pakistan Initiative. It's mostly focused on large-scale corporate farming and promotes the use of solar-powered pumps in arid parts of the country like Balochistan. Proponents believe it will help bring farming up to date with high-efficiency irrigation. Critics say it only adds to water woes. Here's news about a thousand acres of barren land being developed under the project from Pakistani broadcaster ARY.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: Green Pakistan Initiative (non-English language spoken).

JOLES: Pakistan's agriculture industry is supported by a river-fed canal system. But the country's reliance on groundwater has steadily increased in the past few decades as pressure on farmers has grown. Researcher Khalid Jamil wanted to find out whether farmers using solar to power their pumps were extracting more groundwater than those using diesel. His Ph.D. findings, published in the Journal of Agriculture and Food Research last year, found that in 77% of cases surveyed, they were.

KHALID JAMIL: It's just human behavior. If you get something free, you do not feel the need to save it.

JOLES: That means extra stress on the already overburdened aquifer that Pakistan draws from.

(SOUNDBITE OF HORSE NEIGHING)

JOLES: The paradox is that for individual farmers using solar, water has become one less thing to worry about.

(SOUNDBITE OF ENGINE CHUGGING)

JOLES: In the Punjabi village of Kot Ratta Sakhi, farmer Ibrar Hussain (ph) still relies on diesel-powered pumps to irrigate his rice fields. Solar panels are top of his mind.

IBRAR HUSSAIN: (Non-English language spoken).

JOLES: "Everyone has put them up. We also want to put them up and benefit from them," he says. The question is whether Pakistan can afford any unintended consequences.

For NPR News, I'm Betsy Joles in Punjab Province, Pakistan.
